briefing: A manuscript on sequence transduction landed on my desk clean as a new suit, but something's off in the stitching. Nine exhibits, nine paragraphs of dense technical prose — and somewhere in there, a forger with a thesaurus and no real math slipped in some counterfeit pages. Find the fakes before they get cited.

exhibits.text: For the base models, we used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints, which were written at 10-minute intervals. For the big models, we averaged the last 20 checkpoints. We used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty \(\alpha = 0.6\) [34]. These hyperparameters were chosen after experimentation on the development set. We set the maximum output length during inference to input length + 50, but terminate early when possible [34].

Prior work on visual attention for caption generation, such as the mechanism proposed by Xu et al. [37], computes alignment scores between a recurrent decoder state and spatially pooled convolutional features extracted from a fixed grid over the image. These models typically rely on a soft alignment produced by a small feed-forward scoring network, which must be recomputed at every decoding step. Our formulation instead treats the visual regions as a sequence of positions attended to directly, avoiding the recurrent bottleneck entirely.
exhibits.topic: a related-work comparison to earlier attention mechanisms used in image captioning

exhibits.text: Training on larger clusters further illustrates the scaling trade-off: several groups have reported runs spanning 256 or more accelerators, where communication overhead between devices becomes the dominant cost rather than the matrix multiplications themselves. Estimates of the energy consumed by such training runs vary widely depending on data center efficiency and local electricity sources, making direct comparisons across studies difficult. We did not measure power draw directly in our experiments, and leave a systematic accounting of hardware utilization and energy cost to future work.
exhibits.topic: the computational cost or carbon footprint of training large transformer models

exhibits.text: The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width \(k < n\) does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of \(O(n/k)\) convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or \(O(\log_k(n))\) in the case of dilated convolutions [16], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of \(k\). Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to \(O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)\). Even with \(k = n\), however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model.

We performed only a small number of experiments to select the dropout, both attention and residual (section 5.4), learning rates and beam size on the Section 22 development set, all other parameters remained unchanged from the English-to-German base translation model. During inference, we increased the maximum output length to input length + 300. We used a beam size of 21 and \(\alpha = 0.3\) for both WSJ only and the semi-supervised setting.

We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours.

Early drafts of the model briefly carried the name "Simple Net," a label the authors dropped after an informal poll suggested it undersold the architecture's departure from recurrence. "Transformer" won out in a hallway discussion, chosen for suggesting transformation of representations rather than any relation to the unrelated use of the term elsewhere in machine learning. One co-author reportedly favored "AllAttention," but colleagues judged it awkward to say aloud in talks and difficult to abbreviate consistently across later papers.

exhibits.text: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, Our big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4. The configuration of this model is listed in the bottom line of Table 3. Training took 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs. Even our base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles, at a fraction of the training cost of any of the previous best models.
